title: Dinner from a van
text: Street food once meant a quick, greasy compromise; now, in many cities, it {{1}} the most interesting cooking in town. The change has several {{2}}. Rents for restaurant premises have {{3}} beyond what young cooks can pay, while a van or a market stall asks only a {{4}} of the price; cooking in public keeps costs visible and portions honest; and social media {{5}} a good taco truck faster than any newspaper review ever could. The result is a generation of chefs {{6}} everything from Seoul-style corn dogs to Oaxacan mole without ever signing a lease. Cities have been {{7}} to catch up: hygiene rules written for fixed kitchens sit awkwardly with wheeled ones, and planning departments must decide whether a row of food trucks is a nuisance or an attraction. London, Los Angeles and Singapore have all rebuilt their rules around the {{8}} that a kitchen's quality is unrelated to its foundations. The old prejudice — that serious cooking requires four walls — has quietly died, one parking space at a time.

gaps.explanation: 'it serves the most interesting cooking in town' — provides it; sever = cut right through, sentence = pronounce a punishment.
'the change has several drivers' — the forces pushing it; drainer is a sink fitting, and details and delays are not forces.
'rents have ballooned beyond what cooks can pay' — inflated enormously; bellow = roar, belittle = dismiss as unimportant.

gaps.hint: a thin slice (a ___ of the price)
gaps.explanation: 'asks only a sliver of the price' — a tiny share, as a sliver is a thin slice; salver = a tray.
'social media makes a good taco truck' — 'make' here means turn into a success, as in 'make someone's reputation'.
'chefs serving everything from corn dogs to mole' — the participle describes the chefs; swerve = change direction suddenly.

gaps.hint: finding it hard (___ to catch up)
gaps.explanation: 'cities have been struggling to catch up' — having difficulty; straddle = sit across, stumble takes 'over/through' rather than 'to'.
'rebuilt their rules around the premise that…' — the underlying assumption; prowess = great skill.
